word:lxx:L700006.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Aarōnidēs” or “Aaronithis.” It functions as a name rather than as a general description, so its central meaning is identification of the person or group bearing that name. word:lxx:L700143.explanation: “Angith,” also rendered “Anggith,” is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named in four occurrences: three in 1 Kings and one in 1 Chronicles. The available information establishes the name and its locations, but not an additional descriptive meaning. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative.

word:lxx:L700248.explanation: This adverb means “as befits a brother”: it describes something done in a manner appropriate to, or characteristic of, a brother. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea is conduct fitting a brotherly relationship.

word:lxx:L700271.explanation: This noun refers to injury or injustice—wrongdoing that harms another person or violates what is right. It describes a condition or act marked by wrong, rather than fairness or righteousness. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 199 times, most often in the Old Testament portion of the LXX, and its repeated use shows that the idea applies broadly to human conduct and the condition of societies. The word appears in passages ranging from Genesis to the Psalms and later Greek Old Testament writings.

word:lxx:L700385.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “gathering”: an assembling or collected group of people or things. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here, but its basic idea remains a gathering or assembled group.

word:lxx:L701074.explanation: This verb means “nurture” or “bring up,” describing the care and raising of someone. word:lxx:L701157.explanation: This word means a flower, referring to the bloom or visible flowering part of a plant. word:lxx:L701566.explanation: This verb means “unload”: to take a load, burden, or cargo off or out of something. It describes an action rather than a person or object. word:lxx:L701809.explanation: This adjective describes something unbroken or not to be broken. It points to a condition of remaining intact, whole, or resistant to being shattered. word:lxx:L701900.explanation: The word means “soot,” the dark powdery residue left by smoke or fire. It is a noun naming a visible substance, rather than an action or quality. word:lxx:L703678.explanation: This verb means “take good heed to” or “beware of.” It describes deliberate caution—paying close attention so that a person avoids danger, harm, or a serious mistake. word:lxx:L703803.explanation: This word means “roe,” an animal term used as a noun. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:58. word:lxx:L703898.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Dōr” or “Thor,” and functions as the name Dor. word:lxx:L703937.explanation: Engaddi is a proper name, referring to “Engaddi” rather than describing an action, quality, or ordinary object. word:lxx:L704046.explanation: Ezekri is a personal name in the Greek Septuagint (LXX), referring to a particular individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L704121.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “send in” or “bring in.” It describes moving someone or something into a place, emphasizing the action of causing entry. word:lxx:L704352.explanation: Ektyphloō means to blind or make blind.

Its exact force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L705355.explanation: This adjective means “celestial” or “heavenly,” describing something belonging to or associated with heaven rather than the ordinary earthly realm. It identifies the character or setting of what it modifies, so its exact force depends on the noun and surrounding sentence. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: once in Psalms and three times in the Maccabean books. The English rendering “heavenly” appears for one occurrence, supporting the same central meaning.

word:lxx:L705416.explanation: This noun means "desert" or "wilderness": a desolate, uncultivated region rather than a settled place. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe an actual barren landscape, and it may also refer to land left empty or deserted. The word occurs nine times in eight verses, chiefly in Isaiah, with additional occurrences in Ezra and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains a place marked by desolation, emptiness, or wildness.

word:lxx:L705690.explanation: Euskios means well shaded or shadowy.

word:lxx:L705773.explanation: Ephod is the name of a specific biblical object or item, expressed in English by the same word. It functions as a noun rather than an action or description. In the Greek Old Testament, this word appears once, in Judges 8:27. The word itself identifies the ephod, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain what is happening with it there. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Old Testament translation context.

word:lxx:L705805.explanation: Zabdiel, also rendered Zavthil, is a personal name. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, the name occurs twice: once in 1 Chronicles and once in 1 Maccabees. Because the available wording gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, the specific identity and role of each person must be understood from its passage.

word:lxx:L705870.explanation: This word is a proper name referring to Zeb, also rendered Ziv. It identifies a person rather than describing an object, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times across three verses, chiefly in Judges and once in Psalms. Because it is a personal name, its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage rather than from the name itself. The name appears in Judges 7:25, Judges 8:3, and Psalms 82:12.

word:lxx:L705953.explanation: Ēthir, also rendered Ithir, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a specific individual in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 25:28. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, Scripture does not provide enough information here to explain the person’s role or the significance of the name beyond identifying that individual.

word:lxx:L706053.explanation: Thabasōn is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX), referring to a person named in 2 Samuel 24:6. Because it is a personal name rather than a common noun or action word, it does not describe a quality, object, or command. Its significance comes from identifying that individual in the passage. This Greek LXX form occurs once in the available Old Testament corpus.

word:lxx:L706277.explanation: This Greek Old Testament adjective refers to a dead body or carcass. It describes the remains of a creature after life has ended, especially in passages concerned with contact with dead animals and ritual uncleanness. The word occurs 32 times in the Greek Old Testament, with many occurrences in Leviticus and others in books such as Jeremiah and Ezekiel. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a lifeless body or animal carcass.

word:lxx:L706299.explanation: This verb means “make bold” or “embolden”—to give someone courage, confidence, or resolve to act. It describes strengthening another person so that fear or hesitation no longer controls the response. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 3 Maccabees, at 1:22 and 1:26. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains making someone bolder or more courageous.

word:lxx:L706314.explanation: Thronizō refers to being enthroned, expressed as occupying a throne.

word:lxx:L706501.explanation: This word is a personal name, given as “Idouias; Ithoias.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament data, it appears only once, in 1 Chronicles 4:19. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is the personal designation itself.

word:lxx:L706538.explanation: Iezebouth, also rendered Iezevuth, is a proper name preserved as a name rather than translated into an ordinary descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 12:22. The available information identifies how the name is represented, but does not establish from the name alone whether it refers to a person, place, or another named entity. Its precise identification therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L706695.explanation: This word means “18” and identifies the Hebrew letter “tsadhe” in the arrangement of Psalm 118. It functions as an indeclinable number rather than as a word describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 118:137. Its role is therefore structural: it marks the eighteenth position in the psalm’s ordered sequence, while the surrounding verse supplies the content associated with that section.

word:lxx:L706736.explanation: This word refers to mud or slime: wet, soft material that can cling to or cover something. It is a noun, so it names the material itself rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms. Its basic sense remains concrete and physical; the surrounding verse determines how that material is being used in a particular passage.

word:lxx:L706817.explanation: Isia is a proper name, used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented as a common word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship, so its meaning is the personal name itself rather than an idea to define. In this LXX corpus, Isia occurs three times, in two verses of 1 Chronicles, and is rendered “Isia” each time. Its precise identification depends on the surrounding biblical passage.

word:lxx:L706934.explanation: Iōree, also written Ioree, is a proper name—a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 5:13. The available wording identifies the name itself, but does not provide its meaning or explain the person’s role. Therefore, the clearest understanding is simply that Iōree is the personal name preserved in that genealogical or historical record.

word:lxx:L707058.explanation: Kakologeō means to bad-mouth—to revile or speak ill of someone.

word:lxx:L707061.explanation: This verb means to experience something bad or to suffer. It describes undergoing hardship or distress rather than causing harm to someone else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jonah 4:10, and its basic sense is expressed as suffering. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain the specific situation, but the word itself focuses on a person’s experience of something painful, difficult, or harmful.

word:lxx:L707164.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “intoxicated; sleep,” describing becoming drunk or entering sleep. Its basic sense concerns a changed state of awareness or alertness, rather than an action performed on someone else. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Jeremiah 28:39, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples in this corpus. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L707186.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to a nut, especially an almond or an almond blossom. It names the almond-related objects described in Exodus 25, where the word appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, in Exodus 25:33 and 25:34. Its basic meaning is botanical and concrete: a nut or the flower of an almond tree. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular role in either passage.

word:lxx:L707212.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “look down at,” describing the act of directing one’s eyes downward toward something or someone. It expresses a visual action rather than a person, object, or abstract idea. The word appears once in the Greek LXX, in Genesis 18:16, so its normal meaning is established from this single recorded occurrence. The precise force of the action in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its translation context.

word:lxx:L707249.explanation: Katadysis means a descent or going down.

word:lxx:L707335.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “mock at”: to ridicule or treat someone with scorn rather than respect. It describes an active response toward a person or message, not merely private disagreement. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in passages from 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Sirach. Its basic sense remains consistent across these occurrences, while the surrounding verse determines exactly whom or what is being mocked. As a verb, it describes the act of expressing contempt through derision.

word:lxx:L707340.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “rise up against,” describing the act of opposing or standing against someone. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 16:3. Its precise force there belongs to the surrounding passage, but the word itself plainly conveys active resistance or opposition. [p03:word:lxx:L707340:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L707340:occurrences] [p01:word:lxx:L707340:reference:0]

word:lxx:L707403.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “whirl down” or “lead astray.” It describes an action that either sends something downward in a sweeping or turbulent way, or causes someone to depart from the right path. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers 32:13. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense centers on downward movement or misdirection.

word:lxx:L707498.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “overwhelm”: to overcome or overpower someone or something with force. It describes an action rather than a person, quality, or object. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Zechariah 9:15. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of overwhelming or overpowering. This is a distinct Greek LXX word and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament entry.

word:lxx:L707537.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “settlement,” referring to an established place where people live. As a noun, it names the inhabited place itself rather than an action or person. It occurs 29 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, showing a recurring word for a settled dwelling or community. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L707582.explanation: Kedamoth, also rendered Kethamoth, is a proper name for a place. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Deuteronomy 2:26. Because the available information identifies the word as a name rather than a common noun or action, it is best understood as referring to a specific location, not as describing a quality, activity, or spiritual concept. The exact role of Kedamoth in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage and its broader account of Israel’s journey.

word:lxx:L707708.explanation: This word means “bar,” referring to a solid piece used to close, secure, or reinforce an opening. It is a noun naming a physical object rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, including several references in Nehemiah to bars associated with gates and other occurrences in Job and other books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L707731.explanation: This adjective means “called” or “named.” It describes someone or something identified by a particular name or designation. As an adjective, it qualifies a person or thing rather than naming an action. In the Greek Old Testament material represented here, it occurs three times, all in the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its exact force in any one sentence depends on what person or object it describes, but its central idea remains being called or designated by a name.

word:lxx:L707793.explanation: This verb means “bake”: to cook food by heating it, especially prepared food such as bread or cakes. It describes the action of making food ready through baking rather than naming the food itself. This Greek LXX word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both in 2 Samuel 13. Its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its central meaning is the act of baking. [p03:word:lxx:L707793:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L707793:occurrences]

word:lxx:L707876.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “strength”—the quality or source of being strong. It refers to strength as a real capacity, not an action or command. In this corpus, it occurs four times, all in the Psalms, where the wording repeatedly renders the term as “strength.” Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains firm ability, power, or support. The word appears in Psalms 24:14, 27:8, 30:4, and 42:2.

word:lxx:L707894.explanation: This verb means to hurl someone or something down, emphasizing forceful movement from a higher place to a lower one. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 6:10. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its central meaning remains the forceful act of throwing or casting down.

word:lxx:L707919.explanation: This adverb describes something flowing or bursting out like a spring—“like a spring; gushing.” It portrays movement or speech as a forceful, abundant outpouring rather than a slow or measured release. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Maccabees 14:45. Because the verse text is not included here, the surrounding context would be needed to identify exactly what is described as gushing in that passage.

word:lxx:L707942.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to any loud noise or a crash—a sudden, forceful sound. It names the sound itself rather than an action or person. The word occurs once in the Greek text of the deuterocanonical book of Wisdom, at Wisdom 17:17. Without the verse text and its surrounding passage, its exact force there cannot be described further, but its basic meaning remains a distinctly loud or crashing sound.

word:lxx:L708107.explanation: This adjective means “servile”: describing something connected with serving or the condition of a servant. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used 13 times, all within the Old Testament portion of the Greek Septuagint. Its occurrences appear in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, especially in instructions connected with appointed feast days and sacred assemblies. The word therefore identifies a service-related character or duty, while the precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L708284.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “ransoming; redemption”: the act of securing someone’s release by paying the required price or providing the means of release. It can describe redemption in practical situations, such as the recovery of a person or property, and it is also used of God’s saving action. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament, in eight verses. Its central idea is release from an obligation, bondage, or threatened loss through redemption.

word:lxx:L708363.explanation: Maeleth is a proper name, rendered “Maeleth.” It identifies a person, place, or title by name rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Genesis and twice in Psalms. The available references are Genesis 28:9, Psalm 52:1, and Psalm 87:1. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific referent at each occurrence cannot be identified here, but the word’s basic function is clear: it is a named designation, not a descriptive word with a broader ordinary meaning.

word:lxx:L708468.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Manaim” or “Manem.” It identifies a named person or place in the Greek Old Testament, though the available wording alone does not establish which. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX, all in 2 Samuel: 17:24, 17:27, and 19:33. Its precise referent is determined by the surrounding verse and passage rather than by the name itself.

word:lxx:L708529.explanation: Marōdach, also rendered Marothakh, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs twice in this Greek Old Testament corpus, once in Isaiah and once in Jeremiah. Because no broader definition is given for this name, its meaning is best understood as the personal designation itself: “Marōdach; Marothakh.”

word:lxx:L708572.explanation: Maspharath is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament wording of Nehemiah 7:7. It is preserved as “Maspharath,” with the alternate rendering “Masfarath” also recorded for the same name. The available information identifies it only as a name and does not describe the person or place named, so its precise referent must be determined from the surrounding verse. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Nehemiah 7:7.

word:lxx:L708657.explanation: Megistanes means magnates, or great men.

word:lxx:L708774.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means a “post” or “outpost”—a position established for watching, guarding, or maintaining a presence. It occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all within 1 Samuel 14, so its use is concentrated in one narrative setting rather than spread broadly across the corpus. The word refers to a stationed place or position, not to a written message sent through the mail. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L708796.explanation: This verb means “beckon”: to signal or call someone to come nearer. It describes an action directed toward another person, inviting or drawing that person’s attention and approach. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Hosea 11:1–2. The word’s basic meaning remains simple and active: someone beckons another. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and its wording.

word:lxx:L708833.explanation: This verb means to change one’s abode or remove to another place. It describes a person leaving one residence and settling elsewhere, so its central idea is relocation rather than merely traveling briefly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 15:19. The word itself does not specify whether the move is voluntary, forced, temporary, or permanent; those details must come from the surrounding passage. Its basic focus remains the act of changing where one lives.

word:lxx:L708891.explanation: Mēte means “neither” or “nor.” It joins two items that a statement excludes together, forming a negative pair.

word:lxx:L708925.explanation: Minaios, also rendered Mineos, is a proper name—a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, in five verses, including passages in Chronicles and Job. The name itself does not provide a wider definition beyond identifying the person named; the surrounding verse is needed to understand that individual’s role in each passage.

word:lxx:L708950.explanation: Mitra means belt. In the passages, it is placed on the head.

word:lxx:L709023.explanation: Mosollamia is a proper name used to identify a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a personal designation. The name occurs three times in the Greek text of 1 Chronicles, specifically in 1 Chronicles 26:1, 26:2, and 26:9. Its exact significance beyond identifying the person is not established by the available lexical information.

word:lxx:L709081.explanation: This noun means “one initiated”: a person who has been admitted or introduced into something. It identifies the person as the recipient of an initiating process, rather than naming the process itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at Wisdom 12:5. The word’s precise significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is a person who is initiated.

word:lxx:L709315.explanation: Nisa is the name of the first month.

word:lxx:L709360.explanation: Nossia means brood, referring to young birds.

word:lxx:L709441.explanation: Obol means a small unit of money.

word:lxx:L709478.explanation: Oziēlis, also written Ozilis, is a proper name identifying a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 3:27. The available lexical information gives the name itself but does not provide an additional descriptive meaning. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named there.

word:lxx:L709504.explanation: The word means an inhabitant: a person who lives in a particular place. It is a noun that identifies someone by residence, focusing on the fact that the person lives there rather than describing an action. In the Greek LXX, it occurs twice, once in Proverbs and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L709676.explanation: This word means “hoof”: the hard covering at the end of an animal’s foot. It is a noun used to name this part of an animal, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears five times, with occurrences confined to Leviticus and Deuteronomy. For an ordinary reader, it points to the visible hoof itself—the part of the foot being named. Its precise role in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L709694.explanation: This word describes a disease in which the body is drawn backward and becomes stiff—a condition identified as tetanus. It is an adjective, so it describes the bodily condition rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Deuteronomy 32:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning is the severe physical condition itself.

word:lxx:L709719.explanation: Hopōs means how. It can also mean that way, pointing to a way or manner.

word:lxx:L709742.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “get up at dawn.” It describes the action of rising early in the morning, before or as daylight begins. The word is used 54 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its basic sense is a normal description of when someone rises, not a special title or abstract idea. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being described.

word:lxx:L709908.explanation: This Greek LXX noun means “frost,” the thin layer of ice formed when cold air freezes moisture. It names a natural condition rather than an action or emotion. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, appearing in Genesis, Jeremiah, Sirach, and Baruch. Its ordinary meaning remains stable across these occurrences: severe cold expressed through the presence of frost. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what the frost signifies or contributes in any particular passage.

word:lxx:L709931.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “play”: to engage in playful activity or take part in a game or amusement. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs 25 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, with uses extending from Genesis through Sirach. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary sense remains the act of playing or engaging in playful activity.

word:lxx:L710111.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “pose” or “serve”: it describes placing something before someone or presenting it for use. The same basic idea can extend naturally from setting an object in position to making something available or serving it. It occurs 31 times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is used across a range of passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being placed or presented there.

word:lxx:L710256.explanation: This word means working to earn the necessities of life—laboring for one’s daily bread. As a verb, it describes the activity of supporting oneself through work rather than naming a possession or status. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs five times, all in Old Testament passages. Its precise force in any one verse is determined by the sentence around it, but its central sense remains practical livelihood through labor.

word:lxx:L710322.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “cleanse” or “purge away.” It describes removing something unclean or unwanted, whether the cleansing is understood physically or in relation to uncleanness. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament translation, in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Isaiah. Its basic emphasis is decisive removal: what defiles or needs cleansing is taken away. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage and what is being removed.

word:lxx:L710397.explanation: “Peristyle” is a noun naming an architectural feature associated with a building or enclosed space. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs nine times: seven occurrences are in Ezekiel, with one each in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its repeated use in Ezekiel shows recurring architectural language. The available information identifies the term clearly, but without verse text it cannot describe the precise arrangement or function of each peristyle in its individual setting.

word:lxx:L710465.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “squeeze.” It describes the act of applying pressure to something, and it functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Micah and once in Sirach. The word’s precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse context, which is not included here.

word:lxx:L710667.explanation: Poreuomai means to go or travel. Moses asks whether he should go to Pharaoh, and David tells Themar to go to her brother’s house.

word:lxx:L710780.explanation: This verb means to make something clear beforehand or to show it plainly in advance. It describes an action of openly revealing or making a matter understandable before the time when it may otherwise become evident. In the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:14. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

word:lxx:L710843.explanation: This noun means “gateway; entrance,” referring to a passage or access point into a place. It names the entry structure itself rather than an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Amos and once in Zephaniah, showing a specific architectural term used in two prophetic passages. Its exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains a gateway or entrance. [Amos 9:1; Zephaniah 1:9]

word:lxx:L710906.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “run towards”: it describes moving quickly in the direction of someone or something. As an action word, it focuses on active movement toward a destination rather than merely being near it. It occurs 10 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its central sense remains consistent across several kinds of passages. The precise force in any particular verse depends on who or what is being approached and what happens around the action.

word:lxx:L711035.explanation: This adjective describes what is first-born or a firstling—the first offspring or first of its kind in a birth order. It can identify a person or animal as the earliest born, or something regarded as the firstborn. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in Micah and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central meaning remains the first-born or firstling. [1] [2]

word:lxx:L711040.explanation: This adjective means “first-formed” or “first-created,” describing someone or something as formed or created first. It identifies priority in the order of creation or formation, rather than describing a quality such as size, strength, or worth. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, both in the Wisdom of Solomon: Wisdom 7:1 and Wisdom 10:1. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

word:lxx:L711112.explanation: This Greek LXX adjective means “fire-bearing,” describing something that carries, bears, or is associated with fire. It is a descriptive word rather than the name of an object by itself, so the noun it modifies supplies the specific thing being described. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 41:21. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the central idea remains something that bears or conveys fire.

word:lxx:L711149.explanation: Raem is a proper name, also rendered “Rhaem.” As a name, it identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This LXX word occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 2:44. The available information identifies the name and its spelling, but does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the person’s role in that verse. Its precise significance there must therefore be understood from the surrounding genealogy and passage context.

word:lxx:L711264.explanation: This verb means to fan or blow something around. It describes movement caused by air, emphasizing scattering or driving something about rather than simply moving it from one place to another. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 2:35. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and imagery, but the word itself presents the action of fanning or blowing around.

word:lxx:L711286.explanation: This word means “whistling,” describing a sharp, rushing, or hissing sound. It functions as a noun or adjective, so it can name such a sound or describe something marked by it. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs three times, appearing once in Ezekiel and twice in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and image.

word:lxx:L711358.explanation: Sabia or Savia is a proper name, used to identify a person rather than to express an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs twice, once in 1 Chronicles 8:10 and once in 2 Chronicles 24:1. The available rendering preserves the name as “Sabia.” Since no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name’s precise identity and role must be determined from each passage, but its basic meaning is its use as a personal name.

word:lxx:L711361.explanation: This is a proper name, given in the LXX as “Sabchia” or “Savkhia.” It identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, in 1 Chronicles 26:7. Its lexical information supplies the name itself, but does not provide a broader definition, etymology, or description of the person. The precise significance of the name in that verse would require the surrounding passage and verse text.

word:lxx:L711493.explanation: This adjective means “planked; boarded over,” describing something made or covered with boards.
